title: The Tandem Book
text: The Tandem Book Tandem is an experimental, statically typed, C-style language that transpiles to Lua 5.4. It compiles .tdm source files to plain Lua and can run either the generated Lua or ordinary .lua files through its embedded runtime. No separate Lua executable is required. This book is the complete reference for Tandem 0.1. Chapters are ordered so a first-time reader can learn the language from the beginning and jump into the reference chapters as needed. Part I — Getting started Introduction : what Tandem is, how compilation works, and a first taste of the syntax. Getting started : build the compiler, run a first program, and check a file without running it. Part II — The language Types : primitive, table, dictionary, list, tuple, struct, and module types. Variables : declarations, the local and const modifiers, auto inference, and scope. Functions : declarations, parameters, default values, and return types. Statements : assignment, if , while , for , return , and blocks. Expressions : operators, precedence, standard library imports, and the built-in print and printf . Comments : C-style and Lua comment forms. Classes : typed fields, fn methods, self , constructors, new instances, and single inheritance. Part III — Tooling Diagnostics : errors, warnings, and why a single warning blocks compilation. Command line : every CLI mode, output paths, arguments, and exit codes. Rust API : embed the compiler and the Lua runtime in a Rust program. Part IV — Status Limitations : what Tandem does not do yet. The project TODO list tracks planned language, tooling, and runtime work.

title: 1. Introduction
text: 1. Introduction Tandem is an experimental, statically typed, C-style language that transpiles to Lua 5.4. It is inspired by the idea of TypeScript for Lua: keep Lua as the runtime target, but give authors familiar syntax and compile-time type checks. Status: proof-of-concept compiler and runtime, version 0.2.0. This is not production-ready. How compilation works Tandem source files use the .tdm extension. The compiler: lexes and parses the file, type-checks the program, erases all type annotations and modifiers, emits a .lua file next to the source, or to a path you choose, runs the generated Lua in an embedded Lua 5.4 interpreter. The interpreter is Lua 5.4 itself, embedded through mlua with its vendored Lua feature, so a separate lua executable is not needed. Tandem does not bundle a game engine; a host application provides any frame loop and input API. A first taste int playerX = 100; fn movePlayer(int speed = 10) -> void { playerX += speed; } movePlayer(20); if (playerX > 100) { print("Player moved!"); } Types such as int are checked at compile time and erased in the generated Lua, so the output is ordinary readable Lua. How to read this book If Tandem is new to you, read Getting started next, then work through Part II in order. The tooling chapters can be read on their own.

title: 2. Getting started
text: 2. Getting started Prerequisites Install Rust and a working C build toolchain. The C toolchain builds the vendored Lua 5.4 runtime. Build From the project directory: cargo build --release This creates target/release/tandem . Compile and run a program Tandem source files use the .tdm extension. Compilation writes a .lua file next to the source and then executes it: cargo run -- examples/hello.tdm # Compiling examples/hello.tdm # Finished examples/hello.lua Or invoke the compiled binary directly: ./target/release/tandem examples/hello.tdm Choose another output path by passing it as the second argument; the output directory must already exist: cargo run -- examples/hello.tdm build/hello.lua Before compiling, Tandem checks the output path. An existing .lua file is overwritten only if it starts with the Tandem-generated header ( -- Generated by Tandem ... ); otherwise the command refuses to overwrite it. This prevents generated output from replacing hand-written Lua files. Check without running --check parses and type-checks the file without writing or executing any Lua. On success it prints the path: cargo run -- --check examples/hello.tdm # Checking examples/hello.tdm # Finished examples/hello.tdm To install dependencies declared in mlua-pkg.toml , run tandem pkg install from the project directory. See LuaRocks packages for the manifest format and runtime behavior. Split a program across files Use require with Lua's calling syntax. Module paths use / and, preferably, an explicit .tdm or .lua extension: module greetings = require("greetings.tdm"); module helper = require("lua-helper.lua"); print(greetings.hello("Lua")); print(helper.hello("Lua")); The module type declares a binding whose type is inferred from the required file. The Lua-style forms are also supported: local greetings = require("greetings.tdm"); print(require("greetings.tdm").hello("Lua")); A path without an extension is resolved as <path>.tdm , then <path>.lua , then <path>/init.tdm and <path>/init.lua , relative to the main input file's directory. Lua-style dotted names such as lib.math also resolve to lib/math.tdm and the other candidates, for compatibility with Lua packages. Paths beginning with ./ or ../ are treated as explicit relative paths. Every .tdm module reached through require is compiled and embedded into the generated Lua under package.preload . .lua modules are not compiled: they are loaded by Lua at runtime from the input file's directory. Their values are typed dynamically, so use as type when assigning them to statically typed variables. A module that is not found locally is left to Lua's package system, such as modules installed with tandem pkg install . A missing path with an explicit extension or an explicit ./ / ../ prefix is a compile error. As in Lua, a standalone require("greetings.tdm"); only loads the module and does not create a variable. Bind the result with module name = require("..."); or local name = require("..."); to use its exports. See examples/modules.tdm for a program that imports both a Tandem module and a Lua module. Import the standard library Lua's standard library packages are not in scope by default. Import the packages a program uses at the top level, then access their members: import string, math; str upper = string.upper("lua") as str; float root = math.sqrt(16.0) as float; Members of imported packages are dynamic, so an as type assertion is needed when assigning one to a typed variable. Lua's base functions such as tostring and pairs need import base; . See Expressions for the full list. Run ordinary Lua files Pass a .lua file to execute it directly in the embedded runtime. Extra arguments reach the script through Lua's arg table: cargo run -- examples/script.lua first-arg second-arg See Command line for the full CLI reference, including error handling and exit codes.

title: 3. Types
text: 3. Types Primitive types and collection types are checked at compile time and erased in generated Lua. Struct types retain their field names at runtime as ordinary Lua tables. Type Values Lua representation int Integer literals such as 42 number float Decimal literals such as 3.5 number bool true or false boolean str Double-quoted strings string table A Lua table with dynamically typed keys and values table table Key Value A typed table whose keys have type Key ( str or int ) and values have type Value table dict Named, dynamically typed values table list Type Ordered values that all have the given type table tuple Ordered values with a fixed length and a fixed type at each position table void No return value; function return type only nil class name An instance created with new table with a metatable There are no implicit conversions. int and float are distinct static types, even though both use Lua numbers at runtime. auto is not a type of its own: it infers a variable's type from its initializer and locks it. It is valid only in a variable declaration with an initializer. See Variables . A declaration can use the module type to bind a required file: module greetings = require("greetings.tdm"); . The compiler infers the module's exported members from that file. A bare module type outside such a declaration is rejected. Lists use a type after list , for example list int scores = [10, 20, 30]; . List elements must match that type. Lists use square brackets and Lua's one-based indexes. Do not use int[] ; curly braces are for tables and dictionaries, and parentheses are for tuples. A plain table is a generic Lua table whose keys and values are dynamic. A generic table initialized with a table literal keeps the static types of its named fields and positional values for reads through that variable: table t = { count = 1 }; int n = t.count; is checked. Assigning a known field or index validates its value type. Reassigning the whole table makes subsequent reads dynamic again. table Key Value is a statically typed table: Key must be str or int , and every read or write is checked against Value . With str keys, literals use named fields and values can be read with both t.name and t["name"] . With int keys, literals are positional and receive keys 1, 2, 3, and so on. Typed tables still compile to ordinary Lua tables. table str int ages = { alice = 21, bob = 32 }; int bob = ages.bob; ages["carol"] = 17; ages.dave = 4; table int str names = { "zero", "one", "two" }; str one = names[1]; Use dict for named keys, list Type for resizable ordered values of one type, and tuple for an ordered group whose length and positional types are inferred from its first value. These collections compile to Lua tables. Values read from a generic table keep the types of its literal initializer when known; values read from a dict , from a generic table without a literal shape, and values exported by dynamic modules have no statically known type. Dynamic values require an explicit as type assertion to assign them to a statically typed variable, field, or parameter. List reads retain the list's element type, and tuple reads at a constant index retain that position's type. An assertion does not convert or validate the value at runtime. Structs define named fields and their types: struct Point { float x; float y; } Point origin = { x = 0.0, y = 0.0 }; origin.x = 2.0; Struct initializers must provide each field exactly once with a matching value type. Struct declarations are top-level. Their values compile to Lua tables. A class name is also a type. Class instances are created with new and carry field and method types; class values cannot be initialized with table literals. See Classes . table options = { debug = true, retries = 3 }; print(options["debug"]); dict player = { name = "Maria", age = 35, points = 500 }; player.age = 16; list int scores = [10, 20, 30]; scores = [..., 12, ...]; tuple position = (0, 10, 11); tuple position = (4, 10, 11); // same length and positional types position[1] = 5; int x = position[1]; Lists and tuples use Lua's one-based indexing. A list can only be changed by assigning a replacement list; list index assignment is rejected. In a list replacement, each ... keeps the old value at that position, and ... is only valid in lists. Tuples can be reassigned or updated by index only while keeping the original length and type at every position. as type inside a tuple initializer is allowed only for const tuple , which locks the whole tuple. A variable cannot be made const after its first declaration. Lists and dictionaries can be redefined only while their variable is mutable; a list redefinition keeps its element type. Literals Integer literals: 42 , 0 , 100 . Float literals: 3.5 , 9.8 . Decimal literals need digits on both sides of the decimal point, so write 3.5 , not 3. or .5 . String literals: double-quoted, with the escapes \n , \r , \t , \" , and \\ . Boolean literals: true and false . void void is the return type of functions that return nothing. A variable cannot have type void ; the compiler rejects void x = ...; . If a function declaration omits -> type , the return type defaults to void . Type checking Every expression and statement is checked: initializers must match declared types, operands must have compatible types, arguments must match parameter types, and return values must match the declared return type. Type annotations and const / local markers exist only in the source; the generated Lua contains plain values and names.

title: 4. Variables
text: 4. Variables Declarations Declarations use (local) (const) type name = value; , where the parentheses mark optional modifiers. For example: int score = 0; float gravity = 9.8; bool alive = true; str playerName = "Ada"; const int maxLives = 3; local int scoreLimit = 100; (local) (const) str edition = "standard"; list int scores = [10, 20, 30]; tuple position = (0, 10, 11); Every declaration needs an initializer, and the initializer must have the declared type. Reassignments are checked against the variable's current type. To deliberately change that type, annotate the new value with as type : int name = 0; name = "Hello!" as str; name = "Tandem"; // now a str // name = 1; // error: name is now a str Class instances use the special class declaration form: class Player = new player; , optionally with local or const . The class from the new expression supplies the static type. See Classes . The one exception to the type rule is a module binding: module greetings = require("greetings.tdm"); and local greetings = require("greetings.tdm"); infer the module type from require . See Getting started for module imports. Automatic type inference The auto type infers a variable's type from its initializer and then locks it, so later assignments behave as if the inferred type had been written explicitly: auto lives = 3; // inferred as int lives += 1; // lives = "three" as str; // error: cannot change the type of 'auto' variable 'lives' auto greeting = "hi " .. "there"; // inferred as str An auto variable cannot be redefined, and the initializer must have a static type. The type cannot be inferred from a dynamic value such as a member of a standard library package, and using auto in a parameter, field, or return type is an error; it is only valid in a variable declaration with an initializer. as is a type assertion, not a conversion: a statically known value must already have the asserted type. For a dynamic value read from a generic table or dict , from a tuple with an unknown index, or from a dynamic module, as type explicitly asserts its type. The generated Lua does not validate or convert the value at runtime. If different control-flow paths leave a variable with different types, the compiler treats its type as dynamic until an explicit as type assertion is used. A global variable can be retyped at top level; inside a function, use as to read a global whose type changes in the program, and retyping the global itself is rejected. A variable cannot be declared with type void . Collection redefinition list , dict , and tuple declarations may repeat an existing collection name in the same scope to replace its value. Lists keep their declared element type. Tuples keep the length and type at each position inferred by the first declaration. Dictionaries keep the dict type and may contain named fields with different value types. These redefinitions are allowed only for mutable variables. A mutable variable cannot be made const by a later declaration. tuple position = (0, 10, 11); tuple position = (10, 20, 30); // valid // tuple position = ("Hello", 10); // error: wrong length and first element type list int scores = [10, 20, 30]; scores = [..., 12, ...]; The local and const modifiers The local and const modifiers are optional, shown here as (local) and (const) . They may appear in either order, and may be written with or without the parentheses. Thus local const int limit = 10; , (local) (const) int limit = 10; , and const (local) int limit = 10; are all accepted forms. Writing the same modifier twice is an error. local Inside functions and blocks, declarations become Lua locals whether or not local is written. At top level, declarations become Lua globals unless marked local ; top-level locals are visible to functions in the same Tandem file. In generated Lua, top-level local names are hoisted to the top of the chunk. const A const binding can be read like any other variable, but Tandem rejects assignments to it, including compound assignments: const int maxLives = 3; maxLives = 4; // error: cannot assign to constant 'maxLives' maxLives += 1; // error Its initializer must match its declared type. Constness is checked by the Tandem compiler and is erased in generated Lua. A const tuple also locks its elements. Declaring an already mutable collection with const is an error. Scope A declaration is visible from its statement to the end of the enclosing block. Duplicate names in the same scope are rejected except for the collection redefinitions described above. An inner block may shadow a name from an outer scope. Braces create scopes: function bodies, if and while bodies, for bodies, and standalone blocks (see Statements ). { int temporary = 1; print(temporary); } // 'temporary' is unknown here Function parameters occupy the function's scope and may be assigned like any other mutable variable.

title: 5. Functions
text: 5. Functions Declarations Declare functions with fn , typed parameters, and an optional return annotation: fn add(int a, int b) -> int { return a + b; } fn hello() { print("Hello!"); } If -> type is omitted, the return type defaults to void . A non-void function's return statement must include a value of the declared type. A void function may use return; . Every control-flow path of a non-void function must return a value. The check understands return , nested blocks, if statements whose branches both return, and while (true) loops. A function that can fall through to its end reports function 'name' must return a value on every path . Default parameter values Default parameter values must be trailing; a required parameter after a defaulted one is rejected. Calls may omit trailing defaulted parameters. Generated Lua fills them when the parameter is nil : fn greet(str name = "world") -> void { print("Hello, " + name); } greet(); // uses "world" greet("Ada"); // uses "Ada" Defaults are type-checked and evaluated left to right, so a default may refer to preceding parameters. At this stage, a default expression should be a literal or another expression valid in the parameter scope. Calling and forward declarations Argument counts must fall between the number of required parameters and the total number of parameters, and each argument must have the declared parameter type. Function declarations are collected before function bodies are checked, so functions may call declarations that appear later in the source. Function names may not duplicate each other or the built-in names print and printf . Functions are not values in 0.1: they cannot be stored in variables, passed as arguments, or returned. See Limitations . Class methods use the same fn syntax but run with an implicit self ; see Classes .

title: 6. Statements
text: 6. Statements Every statement ends in ; . Blocks use braces. Declarations are covered in Variables ; expressions in Expressions . Assignment Supported assignment operators are = , += , -= , *= , and /= . Targets can be variables, struct or table fields, tuple element indexes, and dictionary or generic table indexes. Compound assignment requires a numeric target when the target type is known. A variable declared const cannot be reassigned. Dictionary fields can be updated, while lists can only be changed by replacing the whole list. Tuple values and elements can change only if the tuple keeps its original length and each position keeps its original type; a const tuple cannot be changed. int score = 0; score = 1; score += 1; score -= 1; score *= 2; score /= 2; list int scores = [10, 20]; scores = [..., 12]; // scores[1] = 12; // error: replace the whole list instead tuple position = (0, 10, 11); position[1] = 5; // valid: position 1 is still an int dict player = { name = "Andy", age = 15, elo = 500 }; player.age = 16; if An if statement takes a parenthesized condition and a block, with an optional else block. The condition must have type bool . if (count == 0) { count += 1; } else { count = 10; } while A while loop also requires a bool condition. A runtime-forever loop such as while (true) { ... } is accepted; a game host normally supplies its own frame loop instead. while (count < 5) { count += 1; } for Numeric for loops include their stop value. The forms are for (name, stop) , for (name, start, stop) , and for (name, start, stop, step) . The first form defaults to start 0 and step 1 ; the second defaults to step 1 . All bounds and steps must be int . A negative step counts downward. The loop variable is an int scoped to the loop body. for (i, 10) { printf("Hello world! {i}"); } A zero step is rejected by the Lua runtime. return A void function may use return; . A non-void function must return a value of its declared return type. The compiler checks each return statement it sees but performs no definite-return analysis, so a function that can finish without returning is not diagnosed. Expression statements An expression on its own is a statement, which is how function calls are written: movePlayer(20); print("Hello!"); Standalone blocks Braces can also create a standalone scope: { int temporary = 1; print(temporary); } This standalone block creates a nested scope and becomes a Lua do ... end block. Its declarations are unavailable after the closing } .

title: 7. Expressions
text: 7. Expressions Forms Supported expressions include literals, variables, function calls, table and list literals, field and index access, type assertions with as type , parentheses, unary ! and - , arithmetic ( + - * / % ), string concatenation ( + , , , and .. ), comparisons ( == != < > <= >= ), and boolean logic ( && || ). A tuple literal is written in parentheses in a tuple declaration. Table literals use { ... } ; generic tables may use named or integer keys. A dict uses named fields inside { ... } . A table Key Value declaration checks the literal against its key and value types: str keys use named fields, while int keys use positional values. List literals use [ ... ] and must match their declared element type. Lists are replaced as a whole, and ... in a replacement preserves the old list value at the same position; ... cannot appear elsewhere. Tuple values use ( ... ) in a tuple declaration. Their length and positional types are fixed by the first value, though values can be updated without changing those types. as type inside a tuple initializer is allowed only for const tuple , which locks the whole tuple. Dictionaries use string keys, lists use integer indexes for reads, and generic tables accept integer or string keys. Values read from a generic table keep the types of its literal initializer when known; values read from dictionaries, from generic tables without a literal shape, and from dynamic modules are dynamic. List elements and tuple positions at constant indexes retain their types. A dynamic value needs an explicit as type assertion before it can be assigned to a typed variable, field, or parameter. as asserts the type but does not convert or validate the value at runtime. list int values = [4, 8, 15]; int first = values[1]; table config = { retries = 3 }; print(config.retries); dict player = { name = "Andy", age = 15, elo = 500 }; tuple position = (0, 10, 11); tuple position = (10, 20, 30); int x = position[1]; Operator precedence From loosest to tightest binding: Operators Associativity , left || left && left == != left < > <= >= left + - .. left * / % left unary ! - prefix Parentheses group subexpressions as usual. The comma operator binds loosest of all, which is why a comma-concatenation passed as a function argument needs parentheses. Arithmetic Arithmetic operands must have the same numeric type; there is no mixing of int and float , and no implicit conversions. Unary - negates an int or a float . % is Lua's remainder operator on the chosen numeric type. Strings + , , , and .. join two strings as well as adding matching numeric values; .. is Lua's concatenation operator. For example: str greeting = "Hello", " world"; str name = "Type" + "Lua"; str file = "notes" .. ".txt"; All three concatenate. Since commas also separate function arguments, wrap a comma-concatenation expression in parentheses when passing it as an argument: print(("Hello", " world")); . Comparisons and logic Equality requires matching non-void types. Ordered comparisons ( < > <= >= ) support matching int , float , or str operands and produce a bool . Boolean operators && and || require boolean operands, as does unary ! . Built-in functions print The built-in print(...) accepts any number of arguments of any type and maps to Lua's print . printf printf accepts one string literal and prints it with {variable} interpolation. Placeholders must name variables in scope. Double braces produce literal braces, as in printf("{{name}} is {playerName}") . An unmatched } , or a placeholder that is not a variable name, is a compile error. int i = 1; printf("Hello world! {i}"); // prints: Hello world! 1 Generated Lua builds the output by concatenating the text with each variable converted by tostring . Standard library imports Lua standard library packages are not in scope by default. Each package must be imported at the top level before it can be used: import string, math; str upper = string.upper("lua"); float root = math.sqrt(16.0); int length = string.len(upper); import may list several packages separated by commas and is only allowed at the top level. Supported packages are string , table , math , io , os , coroutine , utf8 , debug , and package . Importing an unknown package is an error: Unrecognised package 'nope' . Common package members have static signatures. For example, string.upper and string.format return str , string.len returns int , and math.sqrt returns float . Arguments and return values are checked like any other function call. Members without a signature remain dynamic and require an explicit as type assertion. An unknown member is an error such as package 'string' has no member 'nope' . A package name used without its import reports Unrecognised package 'string': import it with 'import string;' . Lua's base functions ( assert , pairs , ipairs , pcall , tonumber , tostring , type , and others) and base values ( _G , _VERSION ) follow the same rule: import base; brings them into scope. Frequently used base functions have static signatures too, such as tostring(any) -> str , type(any) -> str , rawlen(any) -> int , and _VERSION -> str . The Tandem built-ins print and printf described above are always available.

title: 8. Comments
text: 8. Comments Tandem supports C-style line and block comments: // A line comment /* A block comment can span multiple lines. */ Lua comment forms are accepted too: -- for a line comment and Lua long comments such as --[[ ... ]] or --[=[ ... ]=] . The number of = characters in a long comment's opening and closing delimiters must match. Block comments do not nest. These comment forms are accepted in .tdm files. Other Lua syntax belongs in a .lua file, which Tandem can execute directly; .tdm files otherwise follow the Tandem grammar described in this book.

title: 12. Classes
text: 12. Classes Classes group typed fields with methods. Define one with class Name { ... } : class player { str name = "Ada"; int health = 100; constructor(str name) { self.name = name; } fn isAlive() -> bool { return health > 0; } fn damage(int amount) { health -= amount; } } Methods keep the fn keyword. They run with an implicit instance, available as self , which cannot be reassigned. Tandem does not use a this keyword. Fields can be read and assigned directly by name; write self.health when a parameter or local variable has the same name. Field and method names cannot collide. Fields are declared like typed variables and normally need an initializer. The default is evaluated for every new instance before the constructor body runs; in a derived class, the child's field defaults run after base constructors and before the rest of the child constructor. A generic field such as T value; may omit its initializer so the constructor can set it. A class may define at most one constructor , and constructors cannot declare a return type. Creating instances new creates an instance. Parentheses are optional when there are no arguments: local class Player = new player; local class Rival = new player("Grace"); class is a special declaration type: the compiler distinguishes a class definition ( class player { ... } ) from an instance declaration ( class Player = new player; ) by the { or = after the name. The variable takes the static class type of the new expression. local and const may be used as for other declarations. Calling a method uses the same dot syntax as other members; Tandem emits the Lua method call with : : print(Player.name); print(Player.isAlive()); Player.damage(30); print(Player.isAlive()); Class names can also be written directly as parameter, return, or variable types: fn alive(player p) -> bool { return p.isAlive(); } Static and private members Use static for class fields and methods. Static methods have no implicit self ; access static fields through the class name: class Counter { static int value = 0; static fn increment() -> int { Counter.value += 1; return Counter.value; } } int current = Counter.increment(); Static fields are initialized when the class is loaded. Static fields and methods are inherited from class bases. Use private before a field or method to restrict access to the class that declares it: class Account { private int balance = 0; private fn adjust(int amount) { balance += amount; } fn deposit(int amount) { self.adjust(amount); } } Privacy is checked by the compiler. Existing names, including underscore-prefixed Lua-style names such as _balance , keep their existing visibility and behavior. Generics Generic functions infer type arguments from their call arguments. Generic classes require explicit type arguments when constructed and when used as types: fn identity<T>(T value) -> T { return value; } class Box<T> { T value; constructor(T value) { self.value = value; } fn get() -> T { return value; } } Box<int> box = new Box<int>(identity(42)); int value = box.get(); Generic parameters can appear inside existing collection types, for example list T or table str T . Generic class types are invariant: Box<int> and Box<float> are distinct types. Classes are not created from table literals. player { name = "Ada", health = 100 } is rejected; use new player("Ada") instead. Inheritance A class can extend multiple classes and interfaces. The first concrete class base is the primary base for super(...) , super.method(...) , and constructor arguments; later concrete bases are initialized in order and must have no required constructor arguments. Shared ancestors are initialized once. Interfaces add method requirements but no runtime base table. class enemy { str name = "enemy"; int health = 10; constructor(str name) { self.name = name; } fn damage(int amount) { health -= amount; } } class boss extends enemy { int phase = 1; constructor(str name, int phase) { super(name); self.phase = phase; } fn damage(int amount) { super.damage(amount); phase += 1; } } Separate concrete bases with commas. An interface can be listed in extends or in implements ; both forms require the class to provide every declared method with a matching signature. Interfaces may extend other interfaces: interface Named { fn name() -> str; } interface Renderable extends Named { fn render() -> str; } class Sprite extends Asset, Drawable implements Renderable { fn name() -> str { return "sprite"; } fn render() -> str { return "image"; } } The child inherits fields, methods, and static members from every concrete class base. If bases provide the same method, the first base with that method wins; conflicting inherited field types are rejected. Fields declared in the child must not reuse an inherited name with a different type, and overriding a method requires the same parameter and return types. A field and a method cannot share a name anywhere in the inheritance chain. If the child declares a constructor, its first statement must call super(...) with arguments for the primary base constructor. The compiler then initializes later concrete bases before the child's fields and remaining constructor body. If the child does not declare a constructor, its generated constructor accepts the primary base's constructor arguments and initializes each base before the child's own fields. Shared ancestors run once, including in diamond-shaped inheritance. Use super.method(...) to call the primary base implementation of an overridden method. super cannot be used in a class without a concrete base, and it is only available inside instance methods and constructors. A child instance can be used wherever the parent class type is expected: fn hurt(enemy target) { target.damage(5); } hurt(new boss("Dragon", 2)); Method dispatch is dynamic, so this calls boss.damage even though the parameter is typed enemy . Generated Lua Classes compile to ordinary Lua tables and metatables. The class table holds the methods and becomes the __index metatable for each instance. Construction is split into .new , which allocates the instance, and :__init , which initializes fields and runs the constructor: local Hero, player local __tandem_init_state = setmetatable({}, { __mode = "k" }) player = {} player.__index = player function player.new(name) local self = setmetatable({}, player) __tandem_init_state[self] = {} self:__init(name) return self end function player:__init(name) local initialized = __tandem_init_state[self] if initialized["player"] then return end initialized["player"] = true self.name = "Ada" self.health = 100 self.name = name end function player:isAlive() return (self.health > 0) end Hero = player.new("Ada") print(Hero:isAlive()) A derived class points its metatable at its bases, so inherited methods are found in order: boss = setmetatable({}, { __index = enemy }) boss.__index = boss Its __init calls super.__init(self, ...) explicitly, which keeps the instance identity while running the parent initializer: function boss:__init(name, phase) local super = enemy super.__init(self, name) self.phase = 1 self.phase = phase end Fields are normal table entries on the instance. Methods are table entries on the class, found through __index . Tandem emits colon calls for class methods so Lua passes self automatically. No runtime library or Tandem-specific value representation is required. Current restrictions Classes remain module-private. Getters and setters, instanceof , class expressions, computed member names, abstract/final/protected access, and exported classes are not implemented yet. See Limitations and the project TODO list .

title: 9. Diagnostics
text: 9. Diagnostics Tandem reports two kinds of diagnostic: errors and warnings . Both stop compilation. If the compiler produces even one diagnostic, no Lua is generated, written, or run. Errors An error is a violation of the language: a syntax error, a type mismatch, an unknown name, an invalid assignment, and so on. Every statement must end in ; , so omitting one is an error: int x = 1 // error: expected ';' Syntax errors are recoverable. After a malformed statement or declaration the parser skips forward to the next statement boundary, so a single compile can report several syntax errors with their locations. If parsing succeeds, each module is type-checked and the first error in each module is reported. Every parser, lexer, and type error includes a line and column. Locations use one-based lines and columns. Warnings A warning flags code that is technically legal but suspicious. Tandem is deliberately strict: a single warning is fatal, so warnings behave like errors and block code generation. The current warning checks are: a variable shadows a declaration in an outer scope; a local variable or parameter is never used; a statement is unreachable because it follows a return . fn f() -> int { int unused = 1; // warning: unused variable 'unused' return unused; } The compiler collects every warning in a program and reports them together. printf("{name}") placeholders count as uses, so a variable used only inside a printf format is not reported. Reporting Each diagnostic is printed with its severity, its message, and the source path with the location: error: expected ';', found 'int' at line 2, column 1 --> examples/hello.tdm:2:1 warning: unused variable 'unused' --> examples/hello.tdm Messages include the kind of token that was found where the compiler expected something else, for example expected ';', found '}' or expected expression, found ';' . Status messages and diagnostics are colored when the output stream is a terminal. Type errors use the same form. For example, a missing return reports the function's declaration location: error: function 'f' must return a value on every path at line 1, column 1 --> examples/missing-return.tdm:1:1 Because warnings block code generation, tandem writes no .lua file and both tandem and tandem --check exit with a nonzero status whenever a diagnostic is present. The Rust API returns diagnostics as a Vec<Diagnostic> ; see Rust API . Source maps Generated Lua keeps a link back to the Tandem source. Each generated statement and function signature ends with a Lua comment naming the original line and column: x = 1 -- tdm:1:1 if (x > 0) then -- tdm:2:1 print("yes") -- tdm:3:5 end The marker is -- tdm:<line>:<column> . Editors and debugging tools can parse it to map a generated Lua line back to the .tdm file. Nested statements carry their own markers, so the innermost marker on a line is the most precise location.

title: 10. Command line
text: 10. Command line LuaRocks packages Tandem uses mlua-pkg to install pure-Lua LuaRocks packages from their Git repositories. Add a manifest to the project directory: [package] name = "my-project" version = "0.1.0" [deps] penlight = { git = "https://github.com/lunarmodules/Penlight", tag = "1.14.0" } Then run: tandem pkg install At runtime, Tandem loads installed modules from mlua-pkg.lock . For example, require("pl.path") resolves Penlight's path module. Package dependencies are pinned in the lockfile. mlua-pkg reads rockspecs from Git repositories; it does not look packages up by name on luarocks.org, and C modules are not built as part of installation. Synopsis tandem [--memory-limit <bytes>] [--instruction-limit <count>] <input.tdm|script.lua> [output.lua or script arguments...] tandem [--memory-limit <bytes>] [--instruction-limit <count>] --check <input.tdm> tandem --version tandem pkg install [project-dir] The limit flags apply to embedded Lua execution, including the run step after a .tdm file is compiled. Build Install Rust and a working C build toolchain, then build the compiler and its embedded Lua 5.4 runtime from the project directory: cargo build --release This creates target/release/tandem . The Lua runtime is built through the mlua dependency with vendored Lua, so a separate lua executable is not required. Compile and run Tandem source Tandem source files use the .tdm extension. Compilation writes a .lua file next to the source and then executes it: tandem examples/hello.tdm # Compiling examples/hello.tdm # Finished examples/hello.lua Hello, world! Choose another output path by passing it as the second argument: tandem examples/hello.tdm build/hello.lua The output directory must already exist. Before compiling, Tandem checks the target path: an existing .lua file is overwritten only when it starts with the generated header ( -- Generated by Tandem ... ). If the file was not generated by Tandem, the command fails instead of replacing it. When developing in this repository, use Cargo to run the CLI: cargo run -- examples/hello.tdm cargo run -- examples/hello.tdm examples/hello-custom.lua require follows the module graph. Paths use / and may include an explicit .tdm or .lua extension. Without an extension, Tandem tries <path>.tdm , <path>.lua , <path>/init.tdm , and <path>/init.lua relative to the input file's directory. Lua-style dotted names such as lib.math also resolve to lib/math.tdm and the other candidates. Every .tdm file reached from the input is compiled and embedded in the generated Lua under package.preload . Imported .lua files are not compiled or copied; they are loaded by Lua at runtime from the input file's directory. --check parses and checks the same set of files. Check without running --check parses and type-checks the file. It does not write or execute generated Lua, and on success prints the checked path: tandem --check examples/hello.tdm # Checking examples/hello.tdm # Finished examples/hello.tdm cargo run -- --check examples/hello.tdm Run ordinary Lua files Pass a .lua file to execute it directly in the embedded Lua 5.4 runtime. Additional arguments are available to the script through Lua's arg table ( arg[0] is the path, and script arguments start at arg[1] ): tandem examples/script.lua first-arg second-arg cargo run -- examples/script.lua first-arg second-arg The .lua file is run as written; it is not parsed as Tandem or transpiled. Runtime limits Two flags bound execution of Lua code. They may appear before the input path: tandem --instruction-limit 1000000 script.lua tandem --memory-limit 67108864 script.lua --instruction-limit <count> aborts execution after roughly the given number of Lua VM instructions. It is a guard against infinite loops, not a precise time limit; the runtime checks in batches of at most 10,000 instructions. --memory-limit <bytes> sets the Lua allocator limit. Allocation beyond this limit fails with a Lua memory error. Both failures are reported as Lua runtime errors after any Tandem output file has been written, and the command exits with status 1. Diagnostics Source and Lua runtime errors are printed to standard error, and the command exits with a nonzero status: A Tandem diagnostic (error or warning) is printed as error: ... or warning: ... , followed by a --> path:line:column line when the location is known. Because warnings are fatal, either form prevents output generation and exits with status 1. See Diagnostics . A Lua runtime error happens after the output file has been written, so the generated file remains available for inspection. The command exits with status 1. An invalid command line prints the usage message and exits with status 2. Status labels and diagnostics use ANSI colors when the corresponding stream is a terminal; piped output stays plain text. Generated Lua also contains -- tdm:<line>:<column> comments that map statements back to the Tandem source; see Diagnostics . On success the command exits with status 0.

title: 11. Rust API
text: 11. Rust API Tandem uses mlua with Lua 5.4 and its vendored Lua build. The Rust library exposes the compiler and runtime as separate modules: tandem::compiler::compile(&str) -> Result<String, Vec<Diagnostic>> parses and type-checks Tandem source, then returns generated Lua. On any diagnostic it returns the diagnostics instead; because warnings are fatal, a single warning also fails compilation. tandem::compiler::Diagnostic carries a severity ( Severity::Error or Severity::Warning ), a message , and optional line and column values. tandem::runtime::run_file(path) runs an existing Lua file. tandem::runtime::run_source(source, chunk_name) runs Lua source held in memory. tandem::runtime::RuntimeConfig sets optional Lua memory and instruction limits. tandem::runtime::run_source_with_setup(...) runs Lua after a host callback has installed additional Lua APIs. tandem::mlua re-exports the mlua crate so hosts and the runtime use the same Lua types. Run a Lua file from Rust fn main() -> Result<(), String> { tandem::runtime::run_file("script.lua") } For a Lua script that needs command-line arguments, use run_file_with_args : fn main() -> Result<(), String> { tandem::runtime::run_file_with_args( "script.lua", &["first-arg".to_owned(), "second-arg".to_owned()], ) } The runtime sets arg[0] to the chunk name or file path and puts supplied script arguments at arg[1] , arg[2] , and so on. Runtime limits Use RuntimeConfig with the *_with_config functions to bound embedded Lua execution: use tandem::runtime::{self, RuntimeConfig}; fn main() -> Result<(), String> { let config = RuntimeConfig { memory_limit: Some(64 * 1024 * 1024), instruction_limit: Some(10_000_000), }; runtime::run_file_with_config("script.lua", &[], &config) } memory_limit is in bytes and is enforced by the Lua allocator. instruction_limit counts Lua VM instructions and aborts runaway scripts; the runtime checks in batches of at most 10,000 instructions. Both failures are returned as Err(String) . Provide host APIs run_source_with_setup calls a closure with the live Lua value before the chunk runs. The callback can install functions, tables, or globals, and must return Result<(), String> : use tandem::runtime::{self, RuntimeConfig}; fn main() -> Result<(), String> { runtime::run_source_with_setup( "print(greet("Lua"))", "host.lua", &[], std::path::Path::new("."), &RuntimeConfig::default(), |lua| { let greet = lua .create_function(|_, name: String| Ok(format!("Hello, {name}!"))) .map_err(|error| error.to_string())?; lua.globals() .set("greet", greet) .map_err(|error| error.to_string()) }, ) } The standard package search paths and installed mlua-pkg packages are configured before the callback runs. Compile and run source from Rust fn main() -> Result<(), String> { let source = r#" fn greet(str name) { print("Hello, " + name); } greet("Lua"); "#; let lua_source = tandem::compiler::compile(source).map_err(|diagnostics| { diagnostics .iter() .map(|diagnostic| format!("{}: {}", diagnostic.severity.label(), diagnostic.message)) .collect::<Vec<_>>() .join("\n") })?; tandem::runtime::run_source(&lua_source, "generated.lua") } The CLI uses the same API: .tdm input is compiled to a .lua file and then run, while .lua input is executed directly. --check compiles for validation but does not invoke the runtime.

title: 13. Limitations
text: 13. Limitations Tandem 0.2.0 is a small proof of concept. The language does not currently implement: getters and setters, instanceof , class expressions, computed member names, abstract/final/protected access, or class exports from compiled modules; fully static typing for dict values, and for generic table values that were not initialized with a literal; closures or first-class functions; optional types; user-defined operators; static member types for every Lua standard-library function: common members are typed, but the rest remain dynamic. Generic table literal shapes are tracked per variable. They are not propagated through aliases, and a function that mutates a global table can invalidate the shape the checker knows at the call site. For multiple inheritance, the first concrete class base supplies the constructor arguments and super target. Later concrete bases must have no required constructor arguments. Generic class inheritance does not yet support explicitly applying or transforming a base class's type arguments. The parser recovers at statement boundaries, which can discard part of a malformed construct before reporting later errors. Source maps are statement-level comments rather than a byte-accurate mapping, and Lua tracebacks still use the generated file and line numbers. The runtime embeds stock Lua 5.4 and adds no game-engine facilities: a host game engine must provide its own update loop and input API. Planned work is tracked in the project TODO list .
